title: YouTube Script Writer AI: 36 Ready-to-Record Script Beats for Your Next Video
markdown:
# YouTube Script Writer AI: 36 Ready-to-Record Script Beats for Your Next Video

It is 9 p.m., the camera is charged, and the outline is still three bullet points. If you searched for "youtube script writer ai," you probably need a script that gets you recording before the next upload date slips again. The examples below are practical starting points for videos where scripting takes longer than filming.

Each one gives you an opening promise, a sequence of beats, and a close. Replace every `[ADD: ...]` field with a fact you can stand behind. Do not invent a number just because a line sounds better with one.

## Coding and career videos

### 1. Five mistakes self-taught coders make

**Hook:** "You're not bad at coding. You're making these five mistakes."

**Beats:** Name the frustrating symptom. Count down five mistakes with one tiny fix for each. Show a screen or sketch when the idea gets abstract. End by asking viewers to choose one mistake to fix this week.

### 2. Your first portfolio project

**Hook:** "Your first portfolio project should be smaller than you think."

**Beats:** Open with the trap of building a clone too large to finish. Set a one-week constraint. Give three project shapes that prove a skill. Close with the first task to put on a calendar.

### 3. A developer's study routine

**Hook:** "I stopped collecting courses and started finishing one project at a time."

**Beats:** Contrast passive watching with a build-first session. Walk through a session using `[ADD: your study time]`. Show how to save questions for later. End with a next-video tease about debugging without panic.

### 4. Preparing for a junior interview

**Hook:** "The question that exposes an interview answer you memorized."

**Beats:** Put the question on screen. Explain what the interviewer needs to hear. Turn one weak answer into a specific story. Finish with a practice prompt viewers can answer out loud.

### 5. Learning one new framework

**Hook:** "Don't start with the documentation. Start with the page you want to build."

**Beats:** Describe the target page. List the smallest concepts needed to build it. Build the first rough version before polishing. Close by naming the one feature that belongs in version two.

### 6. Debugging a project that feels stuck

**Hook:** "When your project feels broken everywhere, stop changing five things at once."

**Beats:** Freeze the problem in one sentence. Reproduce it. Change one variable and record the result. End with a simple log template viewers can copy.

## Fitness and training videos

### 7. A short home workout

**Hook:** "You have [ADD: your number] minutes. That is enough for this workout."

**Beats:** State who the workout suits. Demonstrate the first move and its common form error. Move through the circuit with rest cues. Close with a clear reminder to adjust for pain or limitations.

### 8. Fixing a squat mistake

**Hook:** "If your squat hurts here, check this before adding weight."

**Beats:** Show the mistake without dramatizing it. Explain one setup change. Show a side-by-side rep. End by asking viewers to film one set and compare it with the cue.

### 9. Returning after a break

**Hook:** "Your first week back should feel almost too easy."

**Beats:** Name the urge to catch up. Set a modest first-session target. Give a three-day outline using `[ADD: your schedule]`. Close with the sign that tells a viewer to repeat rather than increase.

### 10. Protein without a complicated plan

**Hook:** "Before you buy another supplement, look at this meal first."

**Beats:** Put one ordinary meal on screen. Explain how to adapt it to a viewer's preference. Flag that nutrition needs vary. End with a grocery-list prompt using only foods the creator actually eats.

### 11. A warm-up people skip

**Hook:** "This is the two-minute warm-up I do before [ADD: your lift]."

**Beats:** Explain what the lift asks of the body. Demonstrate the two movements. Say what a viewer should feel. Transition into the first work set.

### 12. Tracking progress without obsessing

**Hook:** "The scale is one note, not the whole song."

**Beats:** List two other signals the creator genuinely tracks. Show a blank weekly check-in. Explain when to look for a trend. End with a reminder that one day does not settle anything.

## Personal finance and small-business videos

### 13. A beginner budget reset

**Hook:** "If every payday disappears, start with the last seven days."

**Beats:** Pull up a real, anonymized expense list. Group it into a few useful categories. Pick one change for the next week. Close with the question to ask before the next purchase.

### 14. Pricing a freelance service

**Hook:** "A low price does not make a vague offer easier to buy."

**Beats:** Show the before version of an offer. Add a clear outcome, scope, and limit. Use `[ADD: your price]` only if it is real. End with a short client-facing sentence viewers can adapt.

### 15. A product page teardown

**Hook:** "People cannot buy what they still have to decode."

**Beats:** Put the first screen on display. Identify the unanswered question. Rewrite the first sentence. Close with a check for whether the buyer can say who it is for.

### 16. A week of business tasks

**Hook:** "This is how I choose one revenue task before opening my inbox."

**Beats:** Start with the weekly goal. Show the short task list. Explain why one task goes first. End with a Friday review question.

### 17. Saving for an irregular expense

**Hook:** "A surprise bill is often an expense you forgot to name."

**Beats:** Name one annual cost. Divide it using `[ADD: your interval]`. Show where the amount sits. Close with a list of three expenses to check in the viewer's own life.

### 18. A first sales call

**Hook:** "You do not need a perfect pitch. You need a better first question."

**Beats:** Give the exact question. Show a poor follow-up and a useful one. Explain how to summarize the answer back. End with the next step that should appear in the call notes.

## Cooking and home videos

### 19. A weeknight dinner

**Hook:** "Dinner starts with one pan and the thing already in your freezer."

**Beats:** Show the ingredients at the start. Give the order that prevents waiting around. Include substitutions the creator has tested. End with the finished plate and one storage note.

### 20. Meal prep for people who hate meal prep

**Hook:** "Do not prep five identical meals. Prep five easier decisions."

**Beats:** Prep two base ingredients. Show three ways to change the final bowl. Use `[ADD: your prep time]` only if timed. Close with how to store each part.

### 21. Organizing a tiny kitchen

**Hook:** "The drawer is not too small. It is doing three jobs."

**Beats:** Empty the drawer. Group what belongs elsewhere. Give each remaining item a home. Finish on a quick before-and-after shot.

### 22. A cleaning reset

**Hook:** "Set a timer for [ADD: your number] minutes, then clean this surface first."

**Beats:** Explain why the surface creates the most visual relief. Show the exact order. Stop when the timer ends. Close by naming the next surface for tomorrow.

### 23. Buying less grocery waste

**Hook:** "Your grocery list fails before you get to the store."

**Beats:** Start with what is already in the fridge. Pick meals around it. Show the shorter list. End with one rule for checking the cart before checkout.

### 24. A beginner tool recommendation

**Hook:** "Buy this kitchen tool after you can name the job it will do."

**Beats:** Show the job first. Compare the tool with what most people already own. State the limitation. Close with who should skip it.

## Creator and channel-growth videos

### 25. Planning a video from one comment

**Hook:** "This comment is already your next video outline."

**Beats:** Put the question on screen. Pull out the hidden problem. Turn it into three sections. End with the thumbnail question that matches the video.

### 26. Choosing a video title

**Hook:** "Your title should make one promise your video can keep."

**Beats:** Show a vague title. Rewrite it around the viewer's problem. Offer two alternatives. Close with the thumbnail phrase that does not repeat the title.

### 27. Recording when you feel awkward

**Hook:** "Your first take is allowed to sound like a first take."

**Beats:** Start with a rough clip. Give one setup routine. Show how to record the first thirty seconds twice. End with the part worth fixing in editing and the part worth leaving alone.

### 28. Turning a long video into Shorts

**Hook:** "The best Short is not a trailer. It is one complete answer."

**Beats:** Find one question in the long video. Start with its answer. Cut the setup that only works in the long version. End with the related full-video topic, not a forced cliffhanger.

### 29. A channel about page

**Hook:** "A new viewer should know what they get here in one sentence."

**Beats:** Show a generic description. Replace it with audience, topic, and outcome. Read it aloud. End with a check against the last three uploads.

### 30. A video that did not land

**Hook:** "Before you remake a low-performing video, find the promise it failed to make."

**Beats:** Compare the title, first fifteen seconds, and thumbnail. Name the mismatch. Write a new opening before reshooting. Close with one change to test at a time.

## Tutorials, reviews, and education videos

### 31. A software tutorial

**Hook:** "By the end of this video, you will have [ADD: a specific outcome]."

**Beats:** Show the finished result first. Name the starting point. Break the task into visible steps. Pause where viewers need to make a choice. End with a next project that uses the same skill.

### 32. A product review

**Hook:** "I bought this for one job. Here is what happened when I used it for a week."

**Beats:** State the job and context. Show the best part and the frustrating part. Say who should buy it and who should not. End with the decision, not a sales pitch.

### 33. Explaining a hard concept

**Hook:** "If this term keeps showing up and nobody explains it plainly, start here."

**Beats:** Give the plain definition. Use one concrete example. Address the most likely misunderstanding. Close with the next term viewers need for the topic.

### 34. A before-and-after tutorial

**Hook:** "This is the before. The fix takes [ADD: your number] steps."

**Beats:** Show the problem without hiding it. Walk through each step. Check the result against the starting goal. End with the one adjustment for a different use case.

### 35. Comparing two tools

**Hook:** "These tools solve the same problem, but not for the same person."

**Beats:** Define the job. Compare the one difference that changes the choice. Show one small workflow in each. End with a decision rule viewers can use.

### 36. Answering a recurring question

**Hook:** "I keep getting this question, so here is the short answer first."

**Beats:** Give the answer in one sentence. Explain the exception. Show the next action. Close with the related question worth covering next.

## How to pick and test a script

Pick the example that matches the job your viewer came to solve, not the one with the loudest hook. Say the hook out loud before filming. If it takes a breath too long, cut it. Then check that the first section keeps the promise the hook made.

To test a script, record the same body with two different openings. Keep the topic, thumbnail, and publishing conditions as similar as you can. Compare the early audience-retention pattern in your own channel analytics, then write down what changed. A useful test teaches you something even when neither opening wins by much.

## FAQ

### What should I give a YouTube script writer AI?

Send the topic, the audience, target length, tone, and the facts you can verify. A draft, product brief, or channel idea also works. If a figure is missing, keep it marked `[ADD: ...]` until you can supply it.

### Can I use a generated script word for word?

Use it as a record-ready starting point, then read it aloud. Replace phrases you would not naturally say and check every claim. Your delivery and your real examples are what make the video yours.

### How many hook options should I test?

Start with two or three openings for one video idea. Change the opening, not the whole lesson, so the test gives you a usable comparison.
